policy.humanOutcomeRule: Primary developer evidence can ground what a team intended/tried/changed, but cannot by itself establish Human enjoyment, comprehension, preference or causal outcome.
policy.transferRule: Every experience must carry confounds, transfer risks, a falsifier and a cheap probe. A match suggests an experiment; it never approves or rejects a composition.
policy.successBiasRule: Failure modes, tensions, removals, rejected ideas and production responses are first-class experiences alongside successful combinations.

experienceKinds.TENSION: Mechanisms/goals pull in different directions and require a tradeoff.
experienceKinds.INVERSION: A common convention or causal direction is deliberately reversed.
experienceKinds.SUBSTITUTION: One mechanism/form replaces another way of achieving a function.
experienceKinds.LEARNING_SCAFFOLD: Structure intended to support learning or transfer.
experienceKinds.FAILURE_MODE: Observed or plausible failure boundary worth detecting early.
experienceKinds.PRODUCTION_RESPONSE: Design/production changed in response to evidence, scale or constraints.

experiences.designProblem: How can a shooter discourage passive cover play without simply increasing enemy damage?
experiences.interaction: Recovery resources are pulled toward the enemy and aggression rather than granted primarily by retreat/regeneration, inverting a common safety loop.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Players may evaluate moving toward weakened enemies as a survival option instead of treating distance as the dominant defensive action.
experiences.observedContext: id Software described speed/aggression and taking resources from adversaries as central to push-forward combat.
transferRisks: If enemies cannot be approached safely, the loop may become punitive rather than aggressive.
Resource tuning may dominate the effect more than the nominal mechanic.
experiences.falsifier: Move recovery drops away from enemies or restore passive regeneration; if approach/retreat decisions barely change, the transfer is weak.
experiences.cheapProbe: Graybox one arena with matched damage but compare enemy-bound recovery vs passive recovery; log approach distance and retreat frequency.

experiences.designProblem: How can high combat speed remain actionable rather than becoming visual noise?
experiences.interaction: Fast movement is paired with readable attack intent and immediate feedback so speed can increase decision density without eliminating anticipation.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Players may make repeated micro-commitments based on threat reading rather than freezing or retreating by default.
experiences.observedContext: The push-forward combat talk frames speed and aggression as a coordinated combat direction.
transferRisks: Increasing speed without telegraph readability may collapse agency.
Visual clutter can erase the intended interaction.
experiences.falsifier: Hold damage constant and blur/remove telegraphs; if decision quality and movement pattern do not degrade, claimed coupling is weak.
experiences.cheapProbe: Build two identical enemy patterns, one with clear pre-attack cues and one with ambiguous cues, then compare dodges/commitments.

experiences.designProblem: How can a familiar genre safety convention be replaced without leaving the player defenseless?
experiences.interaction: Cover/regeneration dependence is substituted with movement and enemy-derived recovery, shifting where safety comes from.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Players may plan survival around maintaining combat momentum rather than waiting for a reset state.
experiences.observedContext: The developer account explicitly contrasts push-forward combat with cover/regeneration conventions.
transferRisks: Substitution needs a complete alternative safety economy, not just removal.
experiences.falsifier: Restore strong cover regeneration while keeping all other systems; if behavior is unchanged, cover removal was not structurally important.
experiences.cheapProbe: Toggle only passive regen in the same arena and compare time stationary, encounter duration and recovery sources.

experiences.designProblem: How can precision mechanics be taught without separating tutorial from play?
experiences.interaction: Rooms can isolate a relationship, then recombine it with prior skills while fast retry keeps failure cheap.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Players may infer a mechanic through repeated local attempts and carry it into later recombinations.
experiences.observedContext: The Celeste level-design workshop describes a large staged level-design process and arrangement of challenges.
transferRisks: Over-isolation can make later recombination feel discontinuous.
Fast retry may be necessary for the pedagogy to remain tolerable.
experiences.falsifier: Randomize room order or remove recombination; if later transfer is unchanged, sequencing hypothesis weakens.
experiences.cheapProbe: Create three micro-rooms A, B, A+B and compare ordered vs shuffled exposure.

experiences.designProblem: How can challenge progression and story inhabit the same traversal rather than alternate as disconnected modes?
experiences.interaction: Level progression and narrative/world context are woven into the same spatial journey rather than treated as unrelated payloads.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Players may interpret difficult traversal as part of the character/world arc instead of pure abstract obstacle completion.
experiences.observedContext: The workshop explicitly covers how Celeste weaves story through its world alongside stage design.
transferRisks: Narrative overlay can be decorative if mechanics do not meaningfully relate.
experiences.falsifier: Swap narrative/environment context between mechanically identical sections; if interpretation and route behavior are unchanged, coupling may be weak.
experiences.cheapProbe: Use two identical challenge sequences with coherent vs arbitrary environmental framing and collect post-play interpretation only if Human evidence is later admitted.

experiences.designProblem: How can tactics emphasize planning over hidden-information guessing?
experiences.interaction: Enemy intentions are made legible before resolution while a compact action space supports counter-positioning and displacement.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Players may compare counterfactual board states and spend actions to alter consequences rather than merely maximize damage.
experiences.observedContext: The postmortem centers the long iterative design of Into the Breach and its tactical structure.
transferRisks: Perfect information can reduce tension if action consequences are shallow.
Small-board legibility may not transfer to larger spatial systems.
experiences.falsifier: Hide enemy intent while preserving board/actions; if planning style and displacement value barely change, the interaction is weaker than expected.
experiences.cheapProbe: Prototype a 6x6 deterministic board with visible vs hidden next attacks; count defensive displacement vs damage actions.

experiences.designProblem: How can a tactics game avoid breadth that dilutes legibility and interaction density?
experiences.interaction: Repeated cutting/removal can reduce content/state breadth while preserving interactions that generate consequential choices.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Players may face fewer nominal options but more legible tradeoffs per turn.
experiences.observedContext: The developers report years of cut content and redesign during the postmortem.
transferRisks: Cutting is not inherently beneficial; it only helps if removed content was low-value or duplicative.
experiences.falsifier: Add one previously excluded class of redundant actions; if choice quality improves rather than diffuses, pruning claim fails.
experiences.cheapProbe: Clone a micro-scenario with 4 vs 8 actions where extra actions overlap outcomes; measure dominated choices mechanically before any Human claim.

experiences.designProblem: How can replay variation coexist with tactical accountability?
experiences.interaction: Randomness can be pushed into setup/content selection while immediate tactical resolution remains predictable.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Players may attribute turn outcomes more to visible choices while runs still vary at a larger horizon.
experiences.observedContext: The postmortem explicitly discusses difficulty and RNG design questions.
confounds: exact RNG placement not fully established by summary
transferRisks: Moving randomness to setup may reduce drama in moment-to-moment play.
experiences.falsifier: Inject outcome RNG into otherwise deterministic attacks; if planning and attribution remain unchanged, this boundary is less important.
experiences.cheapProbe: Compare deterministic vs hit-chance resolution on the same tiny board with identical setup seeds.

experiences.designProblem: How can live balance avoid becoming either pure intuition or pure metric optimization?
experiences.interaction: Metrics expose distributions and outliers while qualitative feedback and design judgement preserve intended feel/difficulty.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Production decisions can distinguish statistical imbalance from intentional asymmetry instead of optimizing one scalar.
experiences.observedContext: Mega Crit presented metrics-driven design and balance together with community feedback and feel/difficulty judgement.
transferRisks: Metric targets can Goodhart if treated as objectives rather than evidence.
experiences.falsifier: Blind designers to telemetry or qualitative reports in alternating balance passes; if decisions and outcomes do not diverge, complementarity may be overstated.
experiences.cheapProbe: On a toy deckbuilder, generate balance telemetry and independent play notes, then compare decisions from each evidence source separately and combined.

experiences.designProblem: How can balance preserve discovery/combinatorics without flattening all options to equal aggregate performance?
experiences.interaction: Aggregate metrics can reveal problems, but synergies and situational value create a tension between global equality and local expressive combinations.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Players may choose apparently weaker components because context changes their marginal value.
experiences.observedContext: The source concerns data-driven balancing; this entry preserves its stated evidence limit that metrics do not define universal balance optima.
transferRisks: Without context-sensitive interactions, asymmetry may simply be imbalance.
experiences.falsifier: Normalize every component toward equal standalone value; if build diversity and contextual choices improve, the tension was mischaracterized.
experiences.cheapProbe: Simulate a small card pool with context-dependent multipliers versus equalized standalone values and inspect dominated strategies.

experiences.designProblem: How can repeated configuration chores be removed without hiding the underlying system?
experiences.interaction: Many duplicated request configurations are replaced by named shared groups that synchronize repeated intent across entities.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Players may spend less attention on propagating identical settings and more on planning logistics state.
experiences.observedContext: FFF #382 says playtesting uncovered repeated request updates as a chore and introduced logistic groups.
transferRisks: Abstraction can hide local exceptions or make debugging harder.
experiences.falsifier: Keep copy/paste workflow but improve speed; if shared groups add little, duplication rather than representation may not be core.
experiences.cheapProbe: Prototype ten request nodes with manual copy versus named shared config; compare operations required for a plan change.

experiences.designProblem: When should a previously rejected design be reconsidered?
experiences.interaction: A solution rejected as too edge-case-heavy can become tractable after surrounding systems and implementation capabilities change; current player planning styles can reopen the need.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Designers may legitimately revisit old decisions instead of treating historical rejection as permanent law.
experiences.observedContext: FFF #441 says mixed rockets were previously judged too complicated, then revisited after player behavior and system changes.
transferRisks: Reopening old ideas can waste effort if original constraints still dominate.
experiences.falsifier: Re-evaluate the old design against the original blocker list; if blockers remain unchanged, reopen rationale fails.
experiences.cheapProbe: Maintain a rejected-idea record with blocker predicates; rerun those predicates after a real substrate change before prototyping.

experiences.designProblem: How can engine optimization target problems that matter to actual play rather than synthetic microbenchmarks?
experiences.interaction: Real saves and playtest-scale worlds expose bottlenecks that only emerge from player-built complexity.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Production teams may prioritize optimizations according to observed world structures rather than guessed hotspots.
experiences.observedContext: FFF #421 reports optimization driven by real save/playtest profiles.
transferRisks: Real saves may overrepresent expert extremes; synthetic tests still help isolate cause.
experiences.falsifier: Optimize only synthetic benchmark hotspots; if real-save frame time improves equally, scale-context hypothesis weakens.
experiences.cheapProbe: Profile one synthetic stress test and one real large save; compare hotspot overlap before changing code.

experiences.designProblem: How can onboarding teach a deep system without training players to obey a scripted solution?
experiences.interaction: Teaching is organized around conceptual relations, with constrained tools and help arriving when relevant, instead of reproducing the main-game operation sequence.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Players may build transferable understanding rather than memorizing tutorial steps.
experiences.observedContext: Factorio FFF #284 describes order of concepts, reduced toolsets, creativity, organic learning and delayed help.
transferRisks: Artificial tool restriction can feel punitive if the concept is not exposed clearly.
experiences.falsifier: Teach identical content by step-by-step command sequence; if transfer to a novel logistics task is equal, concept-ordering claim weakens.
experiences.cheapProbe: Create two five-minute onboarding variants, scripted-operation vs concept relation, then test a mechanically new transfer task if Human study is admitted.

experiences.designProblem: How can incremental additions hide cumulative complexity?
experiences.interaction: A full start-to-finish playtest can reveal that individually small additions have accumulated into sufficient content and that further expansion risks overload.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Designers may choose polish/optimization/mod extensibility over more core content after experiencing the complete progression.
experiences.observedContext: FFF #160 reports a 46-hour playthrough, many phase changes, and a conclusion that vanilla content was becoming sufficiently large.
transferRisks: One playthrough cannot establish newcomer overload.
Internal familiarity may understate onboarding cost.
experiences.falsifier: Compare local feature reviews with one full progression audit; if both detect the same saturation signals, full-run value is lower.
experiences.cheapProbe: Periodically run a complete progression with a fixed observation sheet for phase density, repeated chores and unused systems.

experiences.designProblem: How can puzzle rules themselves become manipulable gameplay material?
experiences.interaction: Rules are represented as spatially manipulable word objects, coupling world arrangement with the active rule system.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Players may reason about changing the rules as an action in the same space where consequences occur.
experiences.observedContext: The developer talk describes rules represented as world objects/sentences and iteration around that data structure.
transferRisks: If rule text becomes too broad, search space may become opaque.
experiences.falsifier: Keep identical rule logic but move editing to a detached menu; if puzzle reasoning is unchanged, world-object representation may not matter.
experiences.cheapProbe: Prototype one rule puzzle with in-world word blocks and one with menu toggles while preserving rule transitions.

experiences.designProblem: How can implementation representation change what designers can feasibly explore?
experiences.interaction: A composable rule representation can make new puzzle states and combinations cheap enough to author and iterate.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Designers may search a broader rule space because the implementation turns rule changes into data manipulation rather than bespoke code.
experiences.observedContext: The talk connects iteration to the underlying rule data structure.
transferRisks: A flexible representation can create unusable combinatorics without authoring constraints.
experiences.falsifier: Implement one candidate rule as bespoke code and as grammar data; if iteration cost is similar, representational leverage is weak.
experiences.cheapProbe: Time-box authoring five variants under data-driven vs bespoke representations and compare code/editor changes.

experiences.designProblem: How can repeated run failure support narrative progress rather than interrupt it?
experiences.interaction: Failure returns the player to a social hub where characters remember and react, turning a mechanical reset into a narrative opportunity.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Players may treat defeat as both loss of run state and gain of new relational/story information.
experiences.observedContext: Supergiant describes a living world where characters remember the player over repeated runs and an approach to narrative shaped by Early Access/modular structure.
transferRisks: Without enough reactive variation, hub returns can become repetitive friction.
experiences.falsifier: Replace reactive returns with static hub dialogue; if post-failure route/engagement does not change, coupling weakens.
experiences.cheapProbe: Prototype two short run loops with static vs state-reactive return dialogue; Human interpretation remains unclaimed until studied.

experiences.designProblem: How can a game architecture support repeated external feedback without requiring full completion first?
experiences.interaction: A modular run structure and serial narrative/content delivery were designed with open development in mind, allowing the game to evolve in public.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Production can expose bounded slices while retaining room to add content and react to observed issues.
experiences.observedContext: Supergiant says Hades was designed for Early Access from the ground up and that modular structure and narrative flowed from that idea.
transferRisks: Open development can distort design toward vocal early adopters.
Modularity may constrain forms that need a single complete reveal.
experiences.falsifier: Take a non-modular progression concept and attempt the same update cadence; if revision cost is comparable, architecture coupling is weak.
experiences.cheapProbe: Model content dependencies as a graph and simulate adding/removing one update without rewriting prior progression.

experiences.designProblem: How can dense narrative coexist with players who sometimes want only a short action session?
experiences.interaction: Narrative is available across returns and relationships while the core run can still be entered quickly, creating a tension between narrative depth and low-friction replay.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Players may modulate how much story they consume without losing access to the action loop.
experiences.observedContext: Supergiant explicitly says players can engage with narrative as much as they like or dive into a quick hack-and-slash session.
transferRisks: Optionality can fragment pacing or reduce narrative salience.
experiences.falsifier: Force all dialogue before each run; if session behavior and narrative uptake remain unchanged, optionality may not matter.
experiences.cheapProbe: Create a small loop with skippable/deferrable vs mandatory inter-run narrative and compare mechanical session throughput; Human preference requires later study.

experiences.referenceGame: The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom
experiences.designProblem: How can a sequel create new possibility without discarding a proven world substrate?
experiences.interaction: New abilities multiply with an already rich world, so novelty emerges from new relationships between verbs and existing objects rather than only new map content.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Players may discover materially different routes and constructions because each ability composes with many world objects.
experiences.observedContext: Nintendo describes creating games through multiplication: character abilities multiplied by a world with much to offer.
transferRisks: If world objects do not share consistent affordances, combinability collapses into exceptions.
experiences.falsifier: Give the new ability only bespoke puzzle targets; if solution diversity remains high, broad world coupling may not be necessary.
experiences.cheapProbe: Graybox 12 reusable objects with one combinable verb versus 12 bespoke one-off interactions and enumerate reachable solutions.

experiences.referenceGame: The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom
experiences.designProblem: How can world representation avoid promising interactions the rules refuse?
experiences.interaction: Objects that visually/readably suggest manipulation are made movable/interactive to preserve the player’s causal expectation.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Players may test ideas suggested by the world instead of learning arbitrary exceptions about what is decorative.
experiences.observedContext: Nintendo says they made previously static-looking crates movable because players would expect them to move.
transferRisks: Making everything interactive may be prohibitively expensive or create unwanted exploits.
experiences.falsifier: Keep visual language constant but mark some similar objects noninteractive; if exploration behavior is unaffected, expectation consistency may be less important.
experiences.cheapProbe: Create three visually similar props with consistent vs inconsistent affordances and observe attempted interactions mechanically.

experiences.referenceGame: The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom
experiences.designProblem: How can a sequel avoid feeling like a new map with the same play?
experiences.interaction: Instead of replacing the whole world, the sequel substitutes the protagonist’s action grammar so familiar spaces support different interactions.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Players may re-evaluate known terrain through new verbs rather than only search for unfamiliar geography.
experiences.observedContext: Nintendo explains that a wholly new world might still have felt like the previous game, so Link’s abilities were completely redesigned.
transferRisks: If players lack prior familiarity, the contrast benefit may vanish.
experiences.falsifier: Test the new verb grammar in a familiar graybox and a wholly new graybox; if behavior is identical, familiarity-reinterpretation coupling is weak.
experiences.cheapProbe: Reuse one small map and compare old vs new verb sets before building a new map.

experiences.designProblem: How can simple actions produce deeper planning rather than just broader feature count?
experiences.interaction: Delegated parallel tasks, spatial routes and time create a scheduling problem around otherwise simple action primitives.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Players may prioritize, sequence and parallelize work instead of only executing one verb repeatedly.
experiences.observedContext: Nintendo frames Pikmin around task management and deeper challenge rather than merely more actions.
transferRisks: Poor unit reliability can turn planning into babysitting.
experiences.falsifier: Make tasks strictly serial; if planning depth remains, parallel scheduling may not be central.
experiences.cheapProbe: Prototype three jobs with one worker stream vs two parallel streams and compare reachable schedules.

experiences.designProblem: How can players be prepared for deeper planning without dumping the whole possibility space immediately?
experiences.interaction: Earlier bounded tasks can train scheduling concepts that are later applied to more open multi-task situations.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Players may acquire planning heuristics before facing the highest combinatorial load.
experiences.observedContext: Nintendo describes training players into deeper planning.
transferRisks: Over-scaffolding may delay discovery or make experienced players impatient.
experiences.falsifier: Remove the bounded training sequence and present the same open task first; if planning strategy is unchanged, scaffolding effect weakens.
experiences.cheapProbe: Create one constrained scheduling puzzle followed by an open one; compare with open-only order in a later Human study.

experiences.designProblem: How can a project avoid overcommitting to an inherited genre template too early?
experiences.interaction: Desired player feeling is treated as the search target while mechanics and genre labels remain replaceable implementation hypotheses.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Designers may discard apparently central mechanics when they fail to support the intended experience rather than protect them because of category identity.
experiences.observedContext: Subset Games describes starting from desired feeling, treating mechanics/genre as secondary, and frequently abandoning or altering ideas.
transferRisks: A vague feeling target can become unfalsifiable without concrete behavioral hypotheses.
experiences.falsifier: Freeze genre mechanics first and compare search diversity with a feeling-first prototype portfolio.
experiences.cheapProbe: Write one experience target, generate three structurally different prototypes, and explicitly kill one that fits genre but not target.

experiences.designProblem: How can a small team keep early design flexible?
experiences.interaction: Frequent abandonment/alteration is normalized so prototypes are evidence carriers rather than assets that must survive.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: The team can search more directions before production sunk cost turns into false design authority.
experiences.observedContext: The FTL postmortem emphasizes designing without a pitch and frequent alteration/abandonment.
transferRisks: Throwaway work can become churn if there is no explicit learning question.
experiences.falsifier: Track prototypes with and without a predeclared falsifier; if discard decisions are equally informative, explicit cheap-learning structure may not help.
experiences.cheapProbe: Time-box three variants with fixed learning questions and forbid production-quality assets.

experiences.designProblem: How can a game feel demanding while quietly reducing unfair-feeling failures?
experiences.interaction: Small player-favoring rules can coexist with precise control and a hard presentation, creating tension between literal simulation and perceived fairness.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Players may take aggressive actions because edge cases resolve slightly in their favor without consciously noticing the assistance.
experiences.observedContext: Motion Twin describes small control details and player-favoring rules supporting hardcore feel.
transferRisks: Too much assistance can erase mastery or feel inconsistent.
experiences.falsifier: Disable one forgiveness rule while preserving visible presentation; if outcomes/behavior do not change, that rule may be unnecessary.
experiences.cheapProbe: Add a small coyote/edge forgiveness window to a combat dodge prototype and compare failure boundaries mechanically.

experiences.designProblem: Why can two games with similar nominal verbs feel very different to control?
experiences.interaction: Low-level input/timing/collision/feedback details mediate the player’s experienced control loop even when high-level mechanics are unchanged.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Players may form different timing commitments because the same verb grammar has different execution tolerances.
experiences.observedContext: The developer talk explicitly emphasizes small control details.
transferRisks: Micro-polish cannot compensate for weak high-level decisions.
experiences.falsifier: Match mechanics but vary one timing tolerance at a time; if success windows and action sequences stay identical, chosen detail is not causal.
experiences.cheapProbe: Instrument a single attack/dodge interaction and sweep buffer/cancel windows.

experiences.designProblem: How can open development guide investment without turning the roadmap into a popularity poll?
experiences.interaction: Feedback is used to identify distinctive core spikes worth doubling down on rather than blindly implementing every request.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Production may concentrate on mechanics that generate distinctive observed reactions while treating requests as evidence, not commands.
experiences.observedContext: Unknown Worlds describes listening/iterating on feedback and doubling down on distinct core spikes.
transferRisks: Vocal feedback can overrepresent committed players.
experiences.falsifier: Implement the most requested feature versus strengthen a distinctive core spike; if the former better serves target behavior, spike-priority heuristic fails.
experiences.cheapProbe: Classify feedback by underlying problem and map each to existing core mechanics before accepting feature requests.

experiences.designProblem: How can story motivate exploration without becoming a linear quest rail?
experiences.interaction: Narrative discoveries are distributed through an exploration/survival space so story and material progression can pull through overlapping locations and risks.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Players may choose destinations for both informational and survival/resource reasons.
experiences.observedContext: The postmortem calls out nonlinear story alongside the game’s open-development/core-spike evolution.
transferRisks: Story breadcrumbs can become disguised quest markers if too explicit.
experiences.falsifier: Detach narrative information from resource/exploration locations; if routing remains identical, synergy may be weak.
experiences.cheapProbe: Build a small map where two destinations differ in story/resource overlap and inspect route incentives.

experiences.designProblem: How can an established systemic game be recomposed without merely adding more content?
experiences.interaction: A roguelike-style reset is layered onto immersive-sim verbs so familiar tools operate under changing run constraints.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Players may re-plan known systems each run because reset/variation changes resource and route assumptions.
experiences.observedContext: Arkane describes dismantling existing mechanics, integrating another genre and breaking form.
transferRisks: Reset can undermine authored consequences that immersive sims rely on.
experiences.falsifier: Remove reset/variation while keeping same verbs; if replanning frequency is unchanged, recombination claim weakens.
experiences.cheapProbe: Use one systemic room across three reset seeds with changed constraints and compare viable plans.

experiences.designProblem: How can a follow-on project avoid treating the parent game’s form as immutable?
experiences.interaction: Existing mechanics are treated as reusable parts while the enclosing progression/run structure is allowed to change radically.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Designers may preserve valuable verbs without inheriting every pacing/progression convention of the parent.
experiences.observedContext: The Mooncrash talk explicitly frames the work as dismantling and recombining Prey with another genre.
transferRisks: Form changes can alienate players whose value comes from the original structure.
experiences.falsifier: Prototype one parent mechanic under a radically different progression loop before committing to feature expansion.
experiences.cheapProbe: Recompose a retained mechanic with two alternative session structures and compare mechanical affordances, not popularity.

experiences.designProblem: How can an investigation story preserve uncertainty without hard failure bottlenecks?
experiences.interaction: Hard fail gates are substituted with adaptive progression that can continue through imperfect interpretation while preserving consequences.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Players may commit to interpretations and live with uncertainty rather than reload until a single correct gate opens.
experiences.observedContext: inkle describes few bottlenecks/no fail state and adaptive authored plus procedural glue.
transferRisks: Removing failure can weaken stakes if choices do not reshape later context.
experiences.falsifier: Add one mandatory correct deduction gate; if exploration/interpretation behavior improves, no-fail substitution may not transfer.
experiences.cheapProbe: Prototype a three-clue branch with fail-gate vs consequence-carrying continuation.

experiences.designProblem: How can a large reactive narrative preserve authored voice without hand-authoring every transition?
experiences.interaction: Authored content is connected by procedural/state-aware glue while automated checks catch structural writing problems.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Players may encounter a coherent path assembled from authored pieces that responds to prior investigation state.
experiences.observedContext: The GDC talk describes adaptive authored + procedural glue and automated testing in writing.
transferRisks: Procedural glue can expose seams or flatten pacing.
Automated checks cannot establish story quality.
experiences.falsifier: Replace state-aware glue with fixed transitions; if reachable contradictions do not increase, glue complexity may be unnecessary.
experiences.cheapProbe: Represent five authored scenes plus state predicates and exhaustively enumerate reachable transition contradictions.

experiences.designProblem: How can a mature franchise search beyond incremental feature ideas?
experiences.interaction: A very large idea pool feeds repeated prototype review, letting unusual transformations compete before production commitment.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: The team may discover combinations that would be excluded by a narrow initial design brief.
experiences.observedContext: Nintendo reports 2000+ ideas feeding prototype meetings.
transferRisks: Idea count is not quality; review process can still converge on safe choices.
experiences.falsifier: Compare idea-generation breadth with prototype survival diversity rather than raw idea count.
experiences.cheapProbe: Generate 30 structurally tagged ideas, prototype only 5 maximally different candidates, and track why others die.

experiences.designProblem: How can a familiar platformer produce repeated surprise without replacing its base controls?
experiences.interaction: Temporary transformations can alter local rule/context around a stable movement grammar, creating novelty through recontextualization.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Players may repeatedly re-evaluate familiar verbs under a changed local rule set.
experiences.observedContext: Nintendo’s developer account frames theme-driven transformation as central to the idea/prototype process.
transferRisks: Too-frequent transformation can make rules feel arbitrary.
experiences.falsifier: Keep level geometry but remove temporary transformations; if decisions barely change, the theme is decorative.
experiences.cheapProbe: Use one movement grammar across three short rooms, each altering one environmental rule temporarily.

experiences.designProblem: How can programming concepts become approachable manipulable game-building material?
experiences.interaction: Connectable visual primitives represent behavior and relationships directly, coupling conceptual logic with an inspectable creation surface.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Creators may reason by connecting visible units instead of translating every intention into textual syntax.
experiences.observedContext: Nintendo describes connectable Nodon as approachable game-building primitives.
transferRisks: Visual nodes can become spaghetti at scale.
experiences.falsifier: Implement the same tiny behavior with opaque presets versus composable visible nodes; compare reachable variants mechanically.
experiences.cheapProbe: Provide five primitives and ask whether ten target behaviors can be composed without adding bespoke blocks.

experiences.designProblem: How can novice creators cross the gap from consuming examples to creating independently?
experiences.interaction: Learners can copy and alter completed examples before facing blank-slate creation, progressively shifting authorship responsibility.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Creators may learn causal relationships by modifying known-working systems before inventing full structures.
experiences.observedContext: Nintendo explicitly describes copy/alter before blank-slate creation.
transferRisks: Experienced creators may find forced copying restrictive.
experiences.falsifier: Start novices directly from blank state; if completion/debugging is equal, scaffold benefit weakens.
experiences.cheapProbe: Use one finished microgame, require three modifications, then remove template for a fourth task.

experiences.designProblem: How can creator tooling balance freedom with the risk that novices never finish anything?
experiences.interaction: Guided completion supplies early end-to-end experience before open creation, trading immediate freedom for a working mental model.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Novice creators may gain confidence and system understanding from finishing bounded projects before unrestricted composition.
experiences.observedContext: Nintendo describes guiding learners toward completing functions/projects.
transferRisks: Too much guidance can teach obedience rather than transferable design.
experiences.falsifier: Compare guided project completion with free exploration followed by the same target task.
experiences.cheapProbe: Build a tiny curriculum with one guided whole project and one equivalent component-only tutorial; defer experience claims to Human study.

experiences.designProblem: How can reframing the product change which mechanics count as useful?
experiences.interaction: The design target is substituted from conventional skill-test victory toward generating compelling stories, making setbacks and disproportionate events potentially valuable rather than defects.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Players may evaluate events by narrative consequence as well as optimization success.
experiences.observedContext: Tynan Sylvester explicitly says RimWorld was defined not as a game but as a story generator.
transferRisks: A story-generator frame can excuse arbitrary unfairness if events lack readable causality.
experiences.falsifier: Score one event system only by win-rate fairness versus by resulting state diversity; if design choices do not diverge, framing effect is weak.
experiences.cheapProbe: Create two event schedulers: balanced challenge and narrative-variance; compare generated trajectory diversity mechanically.

experiences.designProblem: Can absence sometimes contribute to play rather than merely represent missing scope?
experiences.interaction: Selected omissions can leave interpretive or systemic space that players mentally fill, inverting the assumption that more explicit features always add value.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Players may infer relationships/stories from partial simulation rather than require every implied system to be implemented.
experiences.observedContext: The RimWorld talk explicitly discusses strategically leaving out features and players engaging with things that are not actually there.
transferRisks: Omission can equally create confusion or disappointment.
experiences.falsifier: Explicitly implement one implied relationship system; if story variety/interpretation increases without cost, omission may not be beneficial.
experiences.cheapProbe: Compare a small simulation with explicit relationship labels versus behavior-only cues; Human interpretation requires later study.

experiences.designProblem: How can teams avoid spending scarce capacity on conventionally mandatory features that do not serve the project’s distinct value?
experiences.interaction: Feature selection challenges category assumptions and asks whether a missing feature actually damages the project’s core value.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Teams may ship without conventionally expected systems if their absence does not break the target experience.
experiences.observedContext: The talk says RimWorld shipped with seemingly critical features missing using a methodology focused on features that matter.
transferRisks: Underbuilding can push hidden costs onto usability/content/community.
experiences.falsifier: For each assumed-mandatory feature, remove it in a prototype and name the exact target behavior that fails; no failure means assumption remains unproven.
experiences.cheapProbe: Run a necessity matrix: feature × claimed player capability, with deletion probe before implementation.

experiences.designProblem: How can an open world direct attention without conventional quest assignment?
experiences.interaction: Explicit mission direction is substituted with diegetic clues and unresolved questions that point toward places and phenomena.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Players may choose destinations because they want to resolve a self-held question rather than satisfy an assigned task.
experiences.observedContext: The GDC talk states the primary goal was open-world exploration driven by curiosity rather than missions or explicit direction.
transferRisks: Some players may become directionless without explicit goals.
experiences.falsifier: Add explicit quest markers/objectives to the same clue network; if route diversity and clue-following remain unchanged, substitution may be less central.
experiences.cheapProbe: Build a three-location mystery map with clue-only vs task-list directions and compare route graph mechanically; Human motivation requires later study.

experiences.designProblem: How can progression persist when the world repeatedly resets?
experiences.interaction: World state resets while player knowledge persists, making learned information itself the durable progression resource.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Players may reach new places or act earlier because they know when/where/how, even though inventory/state does not persist.
experiences.observedContext: The source describes a dynamic solar system in a time loop and player-determined progression through unraveling a nonlinear story.
transferRisks: If knowledge has no actionable consequences, reset becomes repetition.
experiences.falsifier: Give persistent inventory unlocks for the same gates; if route choice is unchanged, knowledge-specific progression may not matter.
experiences.cheapProbe: Prototype one timed gate solvable only after learning a schedule; compare with key-item unlock.

experiences.designProblem: How can narrative content function as navigation infrastructure rather than only reward after gameplay?
experiences.interaction: Narrative clues point to other mysteries/locations, so story information changes the player’s exploration graph.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Players may convert interpretive discoveries directly into new route hypotheses.
experiences.observedContext: The GDC session explicitly examines narrative choices used to inspire, facilitate and reward exploration.
transferRisks: If clues are too explicit they become quests; too vague and they fail to route.
experiences.falsifier: Replace clue relationships with flavor text of equal volume; if navigation graph remains, narrative-routing coupling weakens.
experiences.cheapProbe: Encode a clue graph and remove cross-location references one by one to see which routes become undiscoverable.

experiences.designProblem: How can production infrastructure keep up when design promises broad reactivity?
experiences.interaction: Reactivity at scale forces tools, team structure and representation to evolve; content ambition and production architecture constrain each other.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Designers can only sustain reactive choices that the pipeline can author, validate and render at required throughput.
experiences.observedContext: Larian’s talks describe new storytelling tools and repeated tool/team changes driven by reactivity scale.
transferRisks: Tooling investment can overshoot if reactivity is not central.
experiences.falsifier: Attempt the same reactive content volume with manual/bespoke pipeline; if throughput remains acceptable, tooling pressure is overstated.
experiences.cheapProbe: Model one branching scene with N state variants and measure authoring/check operations under bespoke vs state-driven tooling.

experiences.designProblem: How can a sequel/license preserve recognizability without becoming a compliance exercise against fan expectations?
experiences.interaction: Inherited rules/IP expectations constrain the design while the studio establishes its own vision and new storytelling/system tools.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Players may recognize franchise/rules lineage while encountering systems structured around the new studio’s priorities.
experiences.observedContext: Larian discusses establishing its own vision under inherited expectations.
transferRisks: Breaking expectations can damage identity; preserving too much can block innovation.
experiences.falsifier: List inherited elements and remove one low-value convention while preserving core rule identity; test whether system design gains new options.
experiences.cheapProbe: Run an inheritance matrix: must-preserve / negotiable / accidental convention, then prototype one negotiable inversion.

experiences.designProblem: Why are some game forms feasible for one organization and unrealistic for another even with similar ideas?
experiences.interaction: Organization, tooling and team topology bound the practical design space; production capacity is part of feasibility, not external to design.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: A team may need to change scope or architecture when its organization cannot sustain a desired interaction/content density.
experiences.observedContext: Larian’s postmortems explicitly connect organizational fit, scaling tools/team and development challenges.
transferRisks: Organization should not be used as a reason to reject cheap prototypes of ambitious ideas.
experiences.falsifier: Downscale a reactive concept to the minimum content graph and identify which production constraints persist.
experiences.cheapProbe: Create a throughput budget for authoring/testing one reactive unit before extrapolating total content.

experiences.designProblem: How does procedural generation change design beyond simply producing more maps/content?
experiences.interaction: Procedural generation alters assumptions and interfaces of the systems it touches, so generation and game-system design co-evolve.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Players may encounter relationships/states that were not individually authored but still obey systemic constraints.
experiences.observedContext: The GDC procedural-generation session says procgen changes the design approach of systems it touches.
transferRisks: Generated breadth can overwhelm legibility and testing.
experiences.falsifier: Swap generated relationships for a fixed authored set while keeping mechanics; if system design needs no change, coupling weakens.
experiences.cheapProbe: Generate a tiny history graph and enumerate downstream system assumptions that break under unexpected combinations.

experiences.designProblem: How can procedural content remain debuggable instead of becoming an opaque infinity machine?
experiences.interaction: Concrete generation tools, constraints and inspection methods matter more than abstract claims of endless content.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Designers can iterate on generator behavior by inspecting actual generated cases and constraints.
experiences.observedContext: The source emphasizes concrete tools/methods over abstract infinity claims.
transferRisks: Tooling can still miss rare combinatorial failures.
experiences.falsifier: Remove deterministic seeds/inspection outputs; if debugging cost does not increase, tooling hypothesis weakens.
experiences.cheapProbe: Require seed replay, invariant checks and one visualization for a small generator before adding breadth.

experiences.designProblem: How can a sequel justify itself when the original’s compact completeness is part of its appeal?
experiences.interaction: Expansion pressure conflicts with preserving the predecessor’s identity, forcing explicit search for new possibility rather than automatic content multiplication.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Designers must distinguish identity-bearing constraints from accidental limits of the first game.
experiences.observedContext: Valve’s GDC session is explicitly about creating a sequel to a game that did not need one.
transferRisks: A sequel can succeed through story/content even without deep mechanical transformation.
experiences.falsifier: Prototype one sequel feature that increases content but not possibility and one that creates a new interaction family; compare structural novelty.
experiences.cheapProbe: Map predecessor constraints into identity-bearing vs contingent and attack one contingent constraint.

experiences.designProblem: How can teams expand around a beloved core mechanic without burying it under new systems?
experiences.interaction: New elements are evaluated against whether they extend rather than obscure the identity-bearing core interaction.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Players may encounter new puzzle relationships while still using the central portal reasoning grammar.
experiences.observedContext: The source covers the whole process of extending Portal as a sequel.
transferRisks: Core preservation can become conservatism if every novelty must resemble old puzzles.
experiences.falsifier: Remove portal dependence from one new mechanic; if puzzle identity remains, core-boundary assumption may be too strict.
experiences.cheapProbe: Design one new element with and without required interaction with the core verb and compare reachable puzzle states.

experiences.designProblem: How can two distinct game layers reinforce rather than feel like separate minigames?
experiences.interaction: Campaign-level resource/roster decisions feed tactical missions, whose outcomes feed back into campaign constraints.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Players may value tactical survival differently because losses alter later strategic possibility.
experiences.observedContext: Julian Gollop’s postmortem describes Geoscape and Battlescape as two distinct but reinforcing games.
transferRisks: Weak feedback between layers can make one layer feel mandatory filler.
experiences.falsifier: Break carryover consequences between tactical and strategic layers; if decisions remain unchanged, reinforcement is weak.
experiences.cheapProbe: Prototype a three-mission campaign with persistent roster/resource consequences versus reset-each-mission.

experiences.designProblem: How much procedural variation is useful before generator complexity outweighs replay/production benefit?
experiences.interaction: Procedural assembly is bounded by tactical/production constraints, creating a tension between variation and authored reliability.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Players may see enough spatial novelty to alter positioning without losing readable tactical structure.
experiences.observedContext: Firaxis discusses benefits and costs of moving from handcrafted to procedural level design.
transferRisks: More generation can create invalid/boring tactical spaces.
experiences.falsifier: Increase generator degrees of freedom while holding authored validation fixed; if invalid/low-value layouts rise sharply, bounded variation is supported.
experiences.cheapProbe: Build a small room-module generator with invariants and sweep combination freedom while counting rejected maps.

experiences.designProblem: How can a port preserve the game while radically changing its interface and input?
experiences.interaction: The underlying content/rules are treated as the meal while the interaction plate can be redesigned for phone constraints.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Players may reach equivalent rule decisions through a different control representation.
experiences.observedContext: Lucas Pope describes preserving the meal while changing the plate and substantial UI/input redesign for mobile.
transferRisks: Interface changes can alter timing, friction and therefore the game itself.
experiences.falsifier: Keep desktop UI scaled down versus redesign for touch; compare operation count/errors mechanically.
experiences.cheapProbe: Map each gameplay-relevant action to touch and count precision/occlusion conflicts before implementation.

experiences.designProblem: How can an interface make a large mystery state inspectable without simply listing the solution graph?
experiences.interaction: A book representation organizes deaths, chronology and identity evidence into a navigable structure that becomes part of deduction work.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Players may externalize memory and compare evidence across scenes through a representation aligned with the mystery’s ontology.
experiences.observedContext: Lucas Pope’s devlogs describe the book interface organizing chronology/deaths/identity clues.
transferRisks: A highly thematic interface can add friction if indexing is incomplete.
experiences.falsifier: Replace the book with a flat generic list preserving all data; if deduction operations are unchanged, representation coupling weakens.
experiences.cheapProbe: Prototype the same ten-clue corpus in flat list vs relational notebook and count navigation steps for cross-reference tasks.

experiences.designProblem: How can a solo developer treat failed implementation attempts as design evidence rather than hidden waste?
experiences.interaction: Repeated interface/technical experiments expose constraints that reshape the final information structure over years.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Production knowledge accumulates through revisions even when prototypes are discarded.
experiences.observedContext: The retained devlogs expose implementation experiments and compromises rather than only final rationale.
transferRisks: Visible iteration does not prove each revision improved player experience.
experiences.falsifier: For each discarded prototype, record the exact constraint it revealed; if no transferable constraint exists, do not promote it to a pattern.
experiences.cheapProbe: Maintain an experiment ledger with hypothesis, failure evidence and surviving design consequence.

experiences.designProblem: How can a project survive radical production/design changes without treating the initial form as sacred?
experiences.interaction: Multiple large changes in scope, perspective and style can occur while a smaller identity-bearing intent survives and is re-expressed.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Teams may distinguish product identity from implementation/form choices under severe constraints.
experiences.observedContext: The Saturnalia postmortem describes six years of radical scope/perspective/style changes under financing pressure.
transferRisks: Retrospective coherence can overstate how continuous identity really was.
experiences.falsifier: Name the invariant before and after a forced form change; if no invariant survives, call it a replacement rather than evolution.
experiences.cheapProbe: Take one concept and intentionally realize it in two camera/presentation forms while keeping one explicit experiential invariant.

experiences.designProblem: How can a mature genre gain new decision pressure by importing a loop from another genre?
experiences.interaction: City-building decisions are bounded into repeated runs with reset and meta progression, changing the value of optimization from permanent perfection toward adaptation.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Players may build for short/medium-term objectives and accept impermanence rather than maximize one eternal city.
experiences.observedContext: The postmortem explicitly discusses mixing genres to find underserved value.
transferRisks: Genre combination can become superficial if reset does not change planning.
experiences.falsifier: Remove run reset while preserving city systems; if planning horizon and build priorities stay the same, recombination is weak.
experiences.cheapProbe: Prototype a 20-minute city loop with permanent vs reset settlement and identical economy.

experiences.designProblem: How do team health and business constraints shape the feasible design space rather than merely schedule it?
experiences.interaction: Creative decisions interact with team capacity and commercial survival, creating a tension between novel scope and sustainable iteration.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: A team may choose mechanics/structure that remain supportable rather than maximize theoretical feature breadth.
experiences.observedContext: The developer postmortem links creative, business and team-health decisions during a long indie project.
transferRisks: Invoking sustainability can become an excuse for avoiding high-value experiments.
experiences.falsifier: Separate cheap exploration from expensive production; if a novel concept can be falsified cheaply, team-capacity concerns should not block the probe.
experiences.cheapProbe: Estimate production burden only after a one-day structural prototype, not at idea admission.

experiences.designProblem: How can designers use genre knowledge without inheriting a feature checklist?
experiences.interaction: A taxonomy of survival experiences and player fantasy substitutes for copying the conventional survival-crafting package.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Designers may select or discard familiar features according to the experience relationship they serve.
experiences.observedContext: The GDC talk explicitly says Pacific Drive avoids established formulas using a taxonomy of survival experiences, theme, setting and player fantasy.
transferRisks: A taxonomy can become another rigid checklist if treated as law.
experiences.falsifier: Take one conventional survival feature and remove it; if target survival relationships remain, convention was not necessary.
experiences.cheapProbe: Create a genre-feature matrix where every feature must name the experience relationship it contributes; delete one with no unique contribution.

experiences.designProblem: How can a vehicle change survival play beyond serving as faster movement?
experiences.interaction: The car can act as the locus that binds travel, resource risk, repair and preparation, turning mobility representation into survival system structure.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Players may evaluate route risk partly through vehicle condition and future repair burden rather than avatar health alone.
experiences.observedContext: The primary session describes Pacific Drive’s survival systems/structure and player fantasy centered on its unusual survival form.
confounds: exact car mechanics not fully exposed in source summary
transferRisks: If the vehicle only transports the player, the systemic-locus claim fails.
experiences.falsifier: Replace the vehicle with abstract fast travel while keeping resources/locations; if planning remains, vehicle coupling is weak.
experiences.cheapProbe: Prototype route selection with a persistent damageable vehicle resource versus costless transit.

experiences.designProblem: How can very short competitive matches still support consequential commitment?
experiences.interaction: A short match is paired with a voluntary stakes-escalation/retreat mechanism so commitment depth is not identical to session length.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Players may continually decide not only how to play a position but how much result value to risk on their read.
experiences.observedContext: Second Dinner’s design retrospective highlights three-minute battles and a borrowed doubling-cube mechanic.
transferRisks: Stakes can dominate card play if rewards are too salient.
experiences.falsifier: Remove the snap/retreat layer while keeping match length; if commitment/exit decisions do not change, stakes mechanism may be unnecessary.
experiences.cheapProbe: Implement a 6-turn abstract duel with optional doubling/retreat and compare decision tree size.

experiences.designProblem: How can a small card/action vocabulary remain variable across many short matches?
experiences.interaction: Changing location rules recontextualize card value and spatial allocation without requiring a huge per-match ruleset.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Players may alter placement/timing because the board modifies what an otherwise familiar card means.
experiences.observedContext: The design talk highlights location rules alongside short battles and mechanic borrowing.
transferRisks: Too-volatile locations can reduce deck identity or planning.
experiences.falsifier: Run identical decks on fixed versus changing location modifiers; if card allocation remains unchanged, recontextualization is weak.
experiences.cheapProbe: Use 8 cards and 3 lane modifiers; enumerate how many cards change preferred lane/timing under each modifier.

experiences.designProblem: How can a game communicate theme through rules rather than only text/cutscenes?
experiences.interaction: Resource mathematics, policy tradeoffs and consequences are designed as part of the authorial language, so meaning is carried through action constraints.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Players may encounter an ethical/social idea as a decision pressure embedded in the system rather than as detached exposition.
experiences.observedContext: 11 bit’s talk argues system dynamics and mathematics can carry authorial voice.
transferRisks: Designer intent does not prove player interpretation.
experiences.falsifier: Keep narrative text but neutralize systemic tradeoffs; if intended interpretation remains, systems may not be carrying the meaning.
experiences.cheapProbe: Construct two mechanically equivalent-looking policy choices, one with persistent systemic externalities and one cosmetic; Human interpretation requires study.

experiences.designProblem: How can mechanics, content and story avoid functioning as separate message channels?
experiences.interaction: The player’s action is interpreted through the joint context of systems, content and narrative rather than through one layer alone.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: The same mechanical choice may carry different meaning when its systemic consequences and narrative context align.
experiences.observedContext: 11 bit’s gameplay-language talk argues players experience mechanics/content/story as one integrated experience.
transferRisks: Integration can be asserted post hoc without measurable player effect.
experiences.falsifier: Swap narrative/context labels while holding mechanics fixed; if intended action meaning is unchanged in later Human study, coupling is weak.
experiences.cheapProbe: Document one action across mechanical consequence, content context and narrative interpretation; identify any layer that can be removed without changing the hypothesis.

experiences.designProblem: How can the same RTS intent survive radically different input devices?
experiences.interaction: Different control mappings can preserve shared strategic operations while changing selection/navigation interaction details per device.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Players on each device may reach comparable strategic commands through different motor/control representations.
experiences.observedContext: The UX postmortem centers different input audiences and cross-platform iteration.
transferRisks: Forcing semantic symmetry can underuse device-specific strengths.
experiences.falsifier: Mirror identical low-level controls on both devices; if strategic task completion improves, custom representation may not be needed.
experiences.cheapProbe: Define 5 strategic intents, then count interaction steps/errors under controller-native vs mouse-native mappings.

experiences.designProblem: How can a high-level action fantasy survive translation into low-level implementation?
experiences.interaction: Design works backward from an intended visceral experience into timing, animation, response and presentation details.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Players may perceive the intended power/precision only if low-level feedback supports the same commitment structure.
experiences.observedContext: Capcom’s talk describes working backward from player experience/vision and emphasizes visceral detail.
transferRisks: Aesthetic detail cannot rescue incoherent decision structure.
experiences.falsifier: Keep mechanics fixed and degrade one feedback/timing dimension; if action commitment is mechanically unchanged, perceptual coupling still needs Human evidence.
experiences.cheapProbe: Implement one combo action with two feedback/timing profiles and instrument input/result timing before any feel claim.

experiences.designProblem: When is usability friction an identity-bearing mystery and when is it avoidable confusion?
experiences.interaction: Some unusual/divisive decisions intentionally preserve discovery/strangeness, creating tension with conventional clarity.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Players may learn by probing an opaque system, but excessive ambiguity can become abandonment rather than discovery.
experiences.observedContext: Weather Factory explicitly discusses unusual/divisive decisions in an experimental commercial game.
transferRisks: Intentionality does not make friction good.
experiences.falsifier: Provide an explicit explanation for one opaque relation; if exploration behavior improves without losing discovery, opacity was not necessary.
experiences.cheapProbe: Tag every opaque interaction as mystery-bearing or accidental; prototype clarification of one item from each class.

experiences.designProblem: Can marketing demonstrate a game’s core feeling without revealing its actual content?
experiences.interaction: An external puzzle/ARG can reproduce discovery and secret-solving as a sample of the experience rather than explain features directly.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Prospective players/community may experience a version of the discovery loop before purchase without consuming in-game secrets.
experiences.observedContext: The GDC session explicitly describes using an ARG to communicate what makes Animal Well special without spoiling the game.
transferRisks: External puzzle labor can create unhealthy over-search or exclude solo audiences.
experiences.falsifier: Replace experiential ARG with descriptive trailer copy; if community behavior/understanding is unchanged, experiential marketing may not matter.
experiences.cheapProbe: Design one promotional artifact that uses the target mechanic relationship but none of the game’s actual puzzle answers.

experiences.designProblem: How can communal mystery design accidentally create unhealthy search behavior?
experiences.interaction: If a secret/search space has weak stopping cues, community effort can escalate beyond intended play, turning curiosity into unbounded labor.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Players may keep searching because absence of evidence is interpreted as further hidden content.
experiences.observedContext: The GDC talk explicitly notes community puzzle design can produce unhealthy over-search and requires harm boundaries.
transferRisks: Some communities self-regulate; boundaries may reduce legitimate discovery.
experiences.falsifier: Add explicit completion/stopping cues to a community puzzle; if search persists unchanged, cue hypothesis weakens.
experiences.cheapProbe: For every communal secret, specify a completion witness or bounded search horizon before launch.

experiences.designProblem: Can a guided campaign represent a sandbox core without losing the freedom that makes the core work?
experiences.interaction: The expanding campaign tried to approximate freeplay while adding segmented map/quest constraints; the team judged the resulting playable form less fun than freeplay and cancelled it for 1.0.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Adding guidance that substitutes for self-directed goal formation may change the very decision structure the tutorial/campaign is meant to demonstrate.
experiences.observedContext: FFF #331 explicitly says the expanding campaign introduced unexpected problems and was not fun to play in comparison with Freeplay, leading Wube to abandon the campaign for the 1.0 focus.
transferRisks: A campaign with a different goal than representing freeplay may work well.
The failure cannot be attributed to guidance alone.
experiences.falsifier: A guided version that preserves the same self-authored planning choices as freeplay would weaken the claim that the guidance structure caused the mismatch.
experiences.cheapProbe: Take one sandbox slice and compare self-authored goals with quest-gated progression while holding mechanics constant; inspect which actions/routes become unavailable or externally selected.

experiences.designProblem: Can an onboarding/demo succeed on local learning and appeal metrics while still be the wrong representation of the product?
experiences.interaction: The NPE attracted and pleased new/story-oriented players yet was removed because the team believed its experience was not aligned with the core game and no longer led into the cancelled campaign.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Optimizing a demonstrator for immediate accessibility can select for behaviors/preferences that do not represent the long-horizon product.
experiences.observedContext: FFF #342 says the NPE met many goals and received overwhelmingly positive feedback near the end, but Wube still removed it on product-vision/demo-fit grounds.
transferRisks: Positive onboarding metrics are not evidence of product mismatch by themselves.
Vision alignment can be invoked too vaguely unless the differing player decisions are named.
experiences.falsifier: If users exposed to the demo later encounter the same goal formation, constraint profile and core decisions as the main game, the mismatch claim weakens.
experiences.cheapProbe: List the top decisions in the demo and first hour of core play; compare which goals are authored by the player versus assigned externally before measuring preference.

experiences.designProblem: Should an undesirable state be globally impossible, or should common accidents be prevented while rare cases remain recoverable?
experiences.interaction: A strict no-fluid-mixing concept accumulated exceptional edge-case complexity; Wube replaced it with common-case prevention plus a direct flush/recovery action for complex cases.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Fast recovery can preserve the intended invariant at player scale without encoding every possible prevention edge case into construction rules.
experiences.observedContext: FFF #351 says strict prevention had compounded complexity for over a year and a half, then describes a simplified prevention system plus quick fluid flushing.
confounds: legacy system built before the invariant
transferRisks: Some domains cannot tolerate entering the invalid state at all.
Recovery can hide repeated errors if cost is too low or consequences propagate.
experiences.falsifier: If a bounded implementation can enforce strict prevention with lower complexity and no new interaction friction, the substitution rationale weakens.
experiences.cheapProbe: Implement the same error policy as exhaustive prevention and common-case prevention+undo/flush; count edge-case branches and recovery steps for the exact target system.

experiences.designProblem: When does an apparently organized GUI structure add conceptual and interaction cost instead of clarity?
experiences.interaction: The Character tab duplicated information/actions elsewhere and nested crafting tabs interrupted frequent use; play experience led to tab removal and a flatter default.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Duplicated representations can require users to maintain unnecessary equivalence mappings, while nesting can add mode-selection cost to high-frequency actions.
experiences.observedContext: FFF #363 explicitly calls the Character tab filler/duplication and reports the nested-tab interaction as uncomfortable enough to revert the default.
transferRisks: Tabs can still clarify genuinely distinct tasks.
Flat layouts can overload screens when information density differs.
experiences.falsifier: If duplicated locations reduce search cost for distinct workflows without creating inconsistent state or extra mode switches, the failure pattern does not transfer.
experiences.cheapProbe: Measure one frequent task with duplicated+nested access versus single-location flat access; count mode switches and ambiguous equivalent controls rather than aesthetic preference.

experiences.designProblem: Can a visually strong asset be wrong once repeated at production density?
experiences.interaction: A striking Beacon redesign pulled excessive attention in dense factories and was redesigned again toward lower salience appropriate to its repeated/supporting role.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Visual hierarchy should reflect gameplay/attention priority at the density and zoom where an entity is actually used, not only isolated asset quality.
experiences.observedContext: FFF #351 states the prior redesign was impressive but too visually dominant, especially because Beacons can appear everywhere, leading to a new redesign.
transferRisks: High salience can be desirable for rare critical objects.
Density and camera distance change the relevant representation constraint.
experiences.falsifier: If isolated and dense-context evaluations produce the same attention hierarchy for the target asset, context saturation is not the issue.
experiences.cheapProbe: Render the same candidate at single-object, typical-density and worst-case-density views; compare visual attention target order before polishing details.

experiences.designProblem: Can a useful secondary system make the efficient player strategy bypass the activity that defines the core game?
experiences.interaction: The Auction House solved trade convenience/security but made market acquisition compete with killing monsters for loot; Blizzard ultimately removed it while redesigning itemization/rewards.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: When a secondary system dominates expected reward acquisition, rational use of that system can displace the intended core decision loop even if the feature has independent value.
experiences.observedContext: Blizzard explicitly said the Auction House had benefits and heavy use but undermined Diablo’s core gameplay, then removed it alongside Loot 2.0/Reaper of Souls reward changes.
transferRisks: Trade can reinforce rather than replace a core loop when acquisition incentives are structured differently.
The removal was part of a multi-system redesign, so no isolated effect size follows.
experiences.falsifier: If the secondary market remains available but expected advancement still requires and rewards the core activity at comparable rates, displacement may not occur.
experiences.cheapProbe: Model two reward paths—core activity and external/secondary exchange—and sweep acquisition efficiency until optimal play switches; inspect whether the intended loop remains on the frontier.

experiences.designProblem: Can extensive preproduction create assets/options that later become harder to remove than they are useful?
experiences.interaction: A very large early character list sometimes inspired missions but also produced filler that designers were reluctant to cut after roles/story needs changed.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Preproduction artifacts can become implicit commitments unless each item must re-earn relevance against the evolving game.
experiences.observedContext: Warren Spector’s Deus Ex postmortem says the team created more than 200 characters and that some became filler they were reluctant to cut as mission/story purposes changed.
transferRisks: Broad ideation is not itself the failure; premature attachment is.
Cheap conceptual inventories can remain useful when deletion is culturally/mechanically easy.
experiences.falsifier: If items from a large preproduction inventory are routinely deleted/recombined without affecting decision quality or schedule, the inventory itself is not harmful.
experiences.cheapProbe: Tag every preproduction item with current use, replacement cost and kill date; run a review where unbound items are deleted by default and measure how many later prove necessary.

experiences.designProblem: Do ethical/experiential constraints necessarily reduce creative possibility?
experiences.interaction: Double Fine frames an empathy-focused constraint as expanding what the team could explore while modernizing a legacy narrative platformer.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: A constraint can create new search directions when it changes the questions/design relationships being explored rather than merely forbidding content.
experiences.observedContext: The Psychonauts 2 GDC design postmortem explicitly presents empathy as expanding the design possibility space rather than limiting it.
transferRisks: Vague values do not automatically generate useful constraints.
A constraint can still overconstrain a different target experience.
experiences.falsifier: If adding the constraint only deletes candidates without producing new mechanism/story relations or better discriminators, it is not expanding the local search space.
experiences.cheapProbe: For one design prompt, generate candidates with and without one explicit value constraint; compare not quality scores but the number and structural diversity of new relationship hypotheses created.

experiences.designProblem: When can an inherited long-range vision become harmful after the actual shipped product changes the team’s opportunity landscape?
experiences.interaction: Team 4 continued allocating increasing resources toward a years-old PvE/MMO trajectory after Overwatch became a runaway live success, which the director later described as insufficient focus on the game they already had.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: This is primarily a production/product-topology hypothesis: resource allocation toward an inherited future can reduce the team’s ability to respond to the current player-facing product.
