experiences.observedContext: Aaron Keller explicitly connected Project Titan ancestry, the crawl-walk-run plan and later PvE investment to pulling resources away from the live Overwatch game.
transferRisks: Long-range visions can still be valuable when premises remain current.
A live success can itself create short-termism if every future bet is abandoned.
experiences.falsifier: If the future vision still wins under current product constraints and does not materially degrade current-product obligations, legacy origin alone is not a reason to drop it.
experiences.cheapProbe: For one inherited roadmap thesis, rewrite its original premises using current product evidence and compare current-resource opportunity cost against a fresh alternative.

experiences.designProblem: When should years of work on an ambitious mode be cut rather than completed because the whole cannot cohere?
experiences.interaction: Hero Missions accumulated talents, enemies and mission work but the team reported inability to assemble a polished cohesive experience while scope grew and live-game resources were being pulled away.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: For the shipped product, cancellation can preserve ongoing player-facing capacity when a parallel mode’s completion burden remains structurally open-ended.
experiences.observedContext: The Overwatch director states the team struggled to find footing, tried too many things, lost focus, and ultimately cut Hero Missions rather than continue pulling from the live game.
transferRisks: Cutting too early can destroy option value.
A more bounded Hero Mission scope might have been feasible.
experiences.falsifier: If a bounded slice demonstrates a closed production/quality path within an explicit resource envelope, the open-ended-scope diagnosis weakens.
experiences.cheapProbe: Freeze one end-to-end Hero Mission-equivalent slice and enumerate all content/tool/live-ops obligations required to replicate it N times; test whether the burden scales linearly, sublinearly or explosively.

experiences.designProblem: Can a project with increasingly satisfying gameplay still be the wrong project for its studio?
experiences.interaction: Naughty Dog reported the gameplay/vision becoming more refined while the long-term post-launch support model implied studio-wide resource commitments that conflicted with future single-player development.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: A playable experience can clear local design quality while failing the organization/product-portfolio feasibility boundary required to sustain it.
experiences.observedContext: The studio explicitly framed the decision as a choice between becoming solely live-service oriented and retaining its single-player narrative focus.
transferRisks: Studio identity can become a rationalization if opportunity costs are not quantified.
Different team topology or external support could change feasibility.
experiences.falsifier: If post-launch obligations can be isolated to a bounded team/resource envelope without consuming the rest of the studio, the cancellation rationale no longer transfers.
experiences.cheapProbe: Model the minimum credible 24-month content/ops staffing graph before full production and compare it with the studio’s protected parallel-project capacity.

experiences.designProblem: Does fixing most identified game-side problems imply the reboot is now viable enough to continue?
experiences.interaction: Valve reported being reasonably satisfied with most game-side reboot goals while active player numbers still remained below the level that justified further development.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Product viability depends on adoption/retention/ecosystem variables that are not reducible to whether the redesigned mechanics satisfy internal game-side goals.
experiences.observedContext: Artifact’s team stopped Foundry development after roughly a year and a half of reboot work, while preserving both versions as free playable releases.
transferRisks: Low population does not prove gameplay quality is poor.
A different launch/distribution context could produce a different viability result.
experiences.falsifier: If a product has a credible acquisition/retention path independent of current population and the game-side changes address the bottleneck, current low population alone may not justify stopping.
experiences.cheapProbe: Separate a reboot dashboard into game-side acceptance, acquisition, activation, retention and concurrency; refuse to let completion of one lane substitute for another.

experiences.referenceGame: Final Fantasy XIV (1.0 → A Realm Reborn)
experiences.designProblem: When can an already-shipped online product require a product-level relaunch rather than indefinite incremental repair?
experiences.interaction: Square Enix chose a full relaunch after the unsuccessful 2010 release and rebuilt the MMORPG for A Realm Reborn in roughly two years and nine months.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: When must-have product relationships are blocked by foundation-level dependencies, replacement can be a testable option rather than treating shipped architecture as irreversible.
experiences.observedContext: Naoki Yoshida’s GDC session is explicitly framed around causes of the initial failure, the importance of the relaunch decision, the short rebuild window and business-model commitment.
transferRisks: A relaunch can be costlier than repair when foundations are salvageable.
Brand/community capacity may materially affect relaunch feasibility.
experiences.falsifier: If the critical failed relationships can be restored with bounded patches whose dependency closure remains smaller than replacement, relaunch is not justified by failure alone.
experiences.cheapProbe: Map each central failure to the owning subsystem and compare the dependency closure of repair versus one clean replacement slice before committing to either path.

experiences.designProblem: Can a nearly complete playable build still need a large narrative reset if its parts do not work together?
experiences.interaction: Below Zero was broadly playable except the endgame, yet the team described the living-story attempt as messy and chose a new story while preserving world substrate and selected characters.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Local asset/feature completion does not establish whole-experience coherence; large revisions can preserve validated substrate while replacing the misfitting relationship layer.
experiences.observedContext: Unknown Worlds said the world/features were largely in place but not working in harmony, especially around story motivations and relationships.
transferRisks: Rewrite cost can exceed its value late in production.
A narrative problem may sometimes be fixed locally without changing the whole story.
experiences.falsifier: If the incoherence can be reproduced by one bounded relationship and repaired without invalidating the story graph, whole-story reset is unnecessary.
experiences.cheapProbe: Represent the story as dependency edges over existing world/character assets; identify whether the failure is local or requires rewiring many high-centrality edges before rewriting content.

experiences.designProblem: When does a planning artifact stop representing uncertainty and start coercing the product around obsolete commitments?
experiences.interaction: A roadmap listing many future features created pressure to finish scheduled items regardless of importance, obscured the game’s big picture and contributed to recurring crunch.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Planning detail can create de facto commitment even when formally provisional, reducing the team’s ability to reprioritize based on current product evidence.
experiences.observedContext: Unknown Worlds explicitly described its roadmap as becoming a tyrant and changed to structuring releases around what the game needed/what was ready rather than structuring the game around release columns.
transferRisks: Roadmaps can improve coordination when commitment semantics are explicit.
Low-detail planning can also create ambiguity and hidden dependency risk.
experiences.falsifier: If roadmap entries have explicit expiry/revalidation and teams can drop them without schedule/social penalty, listing future work need not create commitment pressure.
experiences.cheapProbe: Mark each roadmap item as hypothesis, commitment or dependency with an expiry; at the next cycle, measure how many hypotheses can be deleted without escalation.

experiences.designProblem: When should a live game intentionally break its content cadence to restore substrate health?
experiences.interaction: Operation Health delayed planned seasonal content, reduced annual map output and invested in servers, bug fixes, staged deployment and rollback capability.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Protecting release cadence at the expense of unstable substrate can compound player-facing failure; temporarily reducing content throughput may preserve future iteration capacity.
experiences.observedContext: Ubisoft publicly replaced one season with a three-month health push and added TTS→PC→console deployment plus an on/off rollback mechanism.
transferRisks: A health initiative without bounded targets can become indefinite infrastructure work.
Content pauses can damage engagement when substrate health is not actually the bottleneck.
experiences.falsifier: If top incidents are unrelated to deployment/substrate health or can be corrected within normal cadence, a content pause is not supported.
experiences.cheapProbe: Rank current player-facing incident load by recurrence/severity and simulate one release with staged rollout+rollback before cancelling content work wholesale.

experiences.designProblem: Can a foundational shipped combat inventory rule be reversed without treating compatibility with the old model as sacred?
experiences.interaction: Forsaken changed Kinetic/Energy slot semantics to allow powerful Primary or Special weapons and rebuilt ammo distribution around the new foundation, migrating existing weapons into the new model.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: A live system’s foundational taxonomy can be replaced when it constrains desired combat loadouts, provided migration and downstream tuning are treated as part of the change.
experiences.observedContext: Bungie called the slot change fundamental and explicitly retuned damage output and ammo distribution to support it.
transferRisks: Foundation reversal can create widespread balance/migration cost.
Not every disliked rule is a foundation-level bottleneck.
experiences.falsifier: If the desired loadout diversity can be restored through local tuning while preserving the old slot model, a foundation rewrite is unnecessary.
experiences.cheapProbe: Prototype the target loadout choices under old and revised slot taxonomies, then enumerate migration/tuning dependencies before rewriting the live model.

experiences.designProblem: Can multiplayer be deferred as an optional feature and added after the single-player architecture is mature?
experiences.interaction: The team initially imagined co-op but deferred it; later they judged multiplayer would touch nearly everything and cost many months/years, so the shipped game remained single-player.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Some social modes alter authority, state synchronization, simulation and progression deeply enough that deferral changes them from feature work into architecture replacement.
experiences.observedContext: Unknown Worlds explicitly described multiplayer as affecting nearly everything and approaching a restart-scale effort after Early Access architecture had matured.
transferRisks: Modular/network-ready architectures can make later multiplayer cheaper.
This does not show single-player design is preferable.
experiences.falsifier: If the target project can demonstrate authoritative state replication, join/leave, persistence and interaction ownership in one bounded multiplayer slice without rewriting core systems, the counterexample weakens.
experiences.cheapProbe: Before deferring multiplayer, implement one vertical co-op slice spanning state authority, save/load, interaction conflict and reconnect; measure which supposedly local systems require redesign.

experiences.designProblem: Can maximum role-selection freedom externalize team-formation costs onto players?
experiences.interaction: Open role selection allowed flexible compositions but required players with different preferences to negotiate scarce tank/support duties under time pressure, producing pressure and hostility.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: A system can preserve individual option freedom while shifting coordination cost into social bargaining that players did not explicitly opt into.
experiences.observedContext: Blizzard cited tension, pressure, disappointment and hostility in the 40-second team-formation window as reasons for Role Queue.
transferRisks: Flexible groups with established teams may value negotiation.
Fixed role structure can reduce emergent composition creativity.
experiences.falsifier: If teams can retain open selection while coordination costs remain low through incentives, precommitment or group formation tools, freedom itself is not the problem.
experiences.cheapProbe: Run identical team objectives with free role selection versus precommitted roles; count forced role switches, unresolved composition gaps and negotiation actions before measuring preference.

experiences.designProblem: Can a structural matchmaking fix solve composition quality while creating a new bottleneck in population supply?
experiences.interaction: Role Queue reduced composition/social/balance problems, but fixed 2-2-2 matchmaking became constrained by the least-popular role; later 1-2-2 better matched observed role demand and reduced waits.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: When a matchmaking rule requires fixed resource proportions, throughput is bounded by the scarcest role population even if match quality improves.
experiences.observedContext: Blizzard’s 5v5/6v6 retrospective explicitly attributes much queue-time difference to tank-role population ratios rather than total player population.
transferRisks: Different games may have balanced role demand.
Flexible substitution can remove the bottleneck.
experiences.falsifier: If role supply tracks the fixed ratio across realistic demand variation, the queue bottleneck does not transfer.
experiences.cheapProbe: Model matchmaking as a flow network using measured role-arrival rates; identify whether one role caps match throughput before changing team size or incentives.

experiences.designProblem: Can a weak broad penalty deter deliberate social harm without unnecessarily affecting incidental users?
experiences.interaction: The XP penalty was judged insufficient for deliberate leavers while also negatively affecting unintentional leavers; the team moved to escalating queue suspension.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: A punishment whose cost is weak for the target behavior but salient for incidental cases can have poor behavioral selectivity.
experiences.observedContext: Blizzard explicitly described both failure modes before replacing the intervention.
transferRisks: Queue suspensions can also create false positives.
Reward penalties may work in economies where the reward is more valuable.
experiences.falsifier: If target and incidental populations have separable behavior signatures and the existing penalty meaningfully changes target behavior, replacement is not required.
experiences.cheapProbe: Segment repeated deliberate-like leaving patterns from isolated disconnect-like events and simulate penalty cost for each before increasing severity.

experiences.designProblem: Does adding a scarce progression currency create meaningful choice merely because it constrains upgrades?
experiences.interaction: Unstable Cores restricted infusion across power levels but Bungie concluded the restriction did not generate interesting buildcraft decisions and instead inhibited trying/upgrading gear.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Resource friction has design value only when the constrained alternatives create meaningful tradeoffs rather than suppressing experimentation uniformly.
experiences.observedContext: Bungie explicitly said the currency was too restrictive and failed to drive interesting buildcraft, then chose full deprecation.
transferRisks: Scarcity can create meaningful tradeoffs in other systems.
Removing cost can flatten decisions if alternatives genuinely compete.
experiences.falsifier: If spending the currency forces distinct build paths with observable opportunity cost rather than generic delay, the failure pattern weakens.
experiences.cheapProbe: For a representative inventory, enumerate decisions changed by the currency; distinguish branch-changing opportunity costs from uniform time/earn gates.

experiences.designProblem: When does a long-lived universal currency stop being useful enough to justify preserving compatibility with it?
experiences.interaction: Bungie progressively removed Legendary Shards from crafting/vendor costs and phased the currency out, migrating costs toward engrams, Glimmer and other materials.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: A universal currency can accumulate compatibility surface and balance baggage that no longer maps cleanly onto the decisions newer economy systems want players to make.
experiences.observedContext: Official patch/TWID records show staged deprecation across vendor and reward surfaces before final removal.
transferRisks: Universal currencies can simplify economies when their role remains coherent.
Currency removal can merely shift complexity elsewhere.
experiences.falsifier: If the currency still has a unique decision role that cannot be expressed more directly by remaining resources, phaseout may destroy useful structure.
experiences.cheapProbe: Map every spend/source edge for the currency and label the distinct decision it creates; edges with no unique decision become deletion/migration candidates.

experiences.designProblem: Can a clever reusable abstraction for procedural generation cost more than the duplication it removes?
experiences.interaction: Automatic deduplication across noise procedures required expensive dependency analysis; Wube removed procedures entirely and used simpler multi-output programs, improving runtime/compile performance in measured cases.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: For generation tooling, representational reuse is only valuable if dependency management costs remain below the work it saves.
experiences.observedContext: FFF #390 documents the failed deduplication direction, removal of procedures, and reported performance improvements.
transferRisks: Other procedural systems benefit strongly from modular reusable subgraphs.
Performance is not the only reason to retain abstraction.
experiences.falsifier: If reusable procedures materially reduce authoring/error cost without expensive dependency analysis in the target system, simplification may be a regression.
experiences.cheapProbe: Implement one representative generation graph both as reusable procedures and a flattened multi-output program; compare compile time, runtime, dependency complexity and authoring duplication.

experiences.designProblem: When do separately evolved procedural subsystems block coherent control over generated outcomes?
experiences.interaction: Terrain variables and object/resource placement used separate systems; this made desired resource behavior hard to express and contributed to pathological maps, motivating a large refactor into expression trees.
experiences.playerDecisionHypothesis: Procedural flexibility can decrease when related generation dimensions are split across incompatible representations that cannot express joint constraints.
experiences.observedContext: FFF #258 describes strange map outputs, weak setting effects, a separate resource system and the resulting major autoplace refactor.
transferRisks: Unified representations can become over-generalized and harder to optimize.
Pathological outputs may be fixable locally in smaller generators.
experiences.falsifier: If cross-system constraints can be expressed and tested cleanly without representation unification, the refactor need not transfer.
experiences.cheapProbe: Write one cross-cutting generation invariant using the existing representations; count adapters/special cases versus a shared intermediate representation before committing to a rewrite.
